{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOU4GkE88AAAABi5-CGQ", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4BlaE0zhMQPOg", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4BlaE0", "number": 64, "title": "Add a local-AI three-choice quiz game for young children with task-specific model training", "body": "## Goal

Add a **fun, browser-local AI-powered three-choice quiz demo for a 5-year-old** to the Sandbox. The child should be able to play independently with short, simple Japanese questions, large easy-to-tap choices, and pleasant responses. Questions should be generated dynamically so the app is not simply a fixed list of 100 questions repeated forever.

**Primary technical objective:** experiment with a **small, task-specialized local generative model** that can produce age-appropriate quiz questions and plausible options without making a phone such as the **Google Pixel 7a** unusably slow. This is an experimental target, not a claim that the device has already been validated.

Suggested project folder: `projects/kids-ai-quiz/`; use the repository's standard `projects/<slug>/index.html` auto-discovery.

## Product / child experience

- [ ] Show **one question and exactly three large answer choices** at a time; use very short, understandable Japanese, preferably **hiragana-centered**, with digits/visual symbols where helpful.
- [ ] Prioritize familiar topics for a 5-year-old: animals, food, vehicles, colors, shapes, counting, everyday objects and routines. Use intuitive pictures/icons/emoji when clear and unambiguous; don't depend on a child being able to read long strings.
- [ ] Include a simple **Japanese read-aloud** action via browser speech synthesis where supported; provide accessible alternatives when speech synthesis is unavailable and avoid unwanted autoplay.
- [ ] After a choice, give an immediate friendly success/try-again response, with a simple way to continue to another question. No time limits, penalties, pressure, scoring complexity, ads, or accounts.
- [ ] Keep the **layout as the explanation**: big question, three answers, minimal controls, intentional whitespace, simple good-looking animations. No unnecessary labels, introductory essays, AI model badges, motivational taglines, or other UI clutter. Follow the Sandbox's Happy Cat / Walk to Hospital / clock demo minimalist style.
- [ ] Responsive on phones/tablets, touch/keyboard-accessible, readable focus states, reduced-motion support, and no reliance on tiny drag targets.

## Dynamic question generation and correctness

- [ ] Generate **new question variations locally** instead of merely cycling through a fixed prewritten list. Avoid near-identical repeats within a session; vary topics and phrasing naturally.
- [ ] **Exactly one of the three choices must be correct.** Prevent ambiguous questions (e.g. 'What color is an apple?' with red/green/yellow as options), incorrect facts, multiple correct choices, nonsense options, and accidentally misleading explanations.
- [ ] Design an appropriate **verification strategy**. Options include a curated, expandable set of reliable facts/relationships combined with model-generated variations, structural constraints, local deterministic validation and bounded retries. The implementer should research and decide the best design. Do not pretend that a tiny model can guarantee factual accuracy by itself.
- [ ] If validation fails or generation times out, offer a safe, playable fallback (possibly vetted questions), without claiming unlimited novelty or stalling indefinitely. A vetted knowledge base is permitted as a correctness anchor; the **primary experience must not reduce to a fixed list of prewritten questions**.
- [ ] Avoid inappropriate, frightening, adult, private or discriminatory content. Never present uncertain or unvalidated AI output as a trusted educational fact.

## Model research, training, and browser integration — implementation agent decides

**The implementation agent is responsible for the investigation and all technical choices.** Research suitable small local models (Japanese competency, weight/download size, inference speed, runtime compatibility and licensing) and select an effective task-specialization approach. **Do not mandate a specific model, LoRA/QLoRA framework, parameter count, dataset size, distillation strategy, runtime or quantization format.**

- [ ] Investigate **fine-tuning / additional training / distillation or equivalent actual model adaptation**, choose and justify a tractable approach, and **carry out a meaningful task-specific adaptation experiment** for generating children's three-choice quiz items. Prompt engineering alone is not the requested experiment.
- [ ] Prepare and quality-check appropriate supervised/training data, including **correct and unambiguous** options, age-appropriate Japanese phrasing, varied topics and negative examples of invalid quizzes. Use material with documented provenance and compatible training/model licenses. No unauthorized private user data or scraping of copyrighted content.
- [ ] Make training reproducible (scripts/configuration/data preparation, pinned dependencies and model versions, artifact/checksum or durable versioned download, and a short report of what was tried, what failed and why). Do not commit huge weights or training-only frameworks into the public static project folders/repository unnecessarily.
- [ ] Run **all inference in the browser**, using WebGPU and/or WebAssembly as genuinely supported. No remote text-generation API, server inference, paid online AI, Cloudflare Workers/DO, user account or backend storage. Downloading pinned public model/runtime assets as static files is okay; clearly document first-use size and caching.
- [ ] Prefer a low-memory, modest-download, responsive implementation suited to Pixel 7a-class Android browsers. Bound generation time, token count, memory, concurrency and retries. Provide a clear loading/failure state and a safe fallback for unsupported hardware. Don't claim real-device support based only on desktop tests.
- [ ] Keep model/training architecture separate from the game UI so later model experiments can be compared or rolled back easily.
- [ ] **No paid training hardware, subscription, API, or cloud spending without explicit approval.** Use available local/free resources and disclose blockers or limitations honestly.

## Comparison and validation

- [ ] Construct representative **held-out** Japanese quiz tests not used in training. Measure three-choice JSON/structured-output validity, exactly-one-correct-answer rate after independent validation, age-appropriateness, relevance, variety/near-duplicate rate, latency and memory/download costs.
- [ ] Compare a reasonable untuned baseline with the specialized model or approach under comparable conditions, and record actual examples (both acceptable and failed) without inflating metrics. Evaluate gameplay usability, not merely whether the model emits syntax.
- [ ] Automated tests must cover answer correctness checks, handling of nonsense/ambiguous/unsafe output, repeated questions, model loading/errors/timeouts, generation fallback, start/stop/retry, optional speech, mobile viewport and keyboard/touch interactions.
- [ ] Ensure site gallery screenshot generation produces an attractive **inert preview without downloading weights or performing inference**, and the existing Sandbox build/deploy tests remain green.
- [ ] No telemetry, uploading child interactions, or persistence of private data; no camera/mic permissions are needed for this game.

## Acceptance criteria — entirely agent-verifiable

**These are the only merge/close gates. Implementation and review must be unblocked by the lack of a physical Pixel 7a or a human child tester.**

1. The new project builds and appears automatically in the Sandbox gallery. Its normal UI is a polished, minimal Japanese three-choice quiz that can be played with touch and keyboard.
2. A genuinely task-adapted small local model is researched, trained/adapted, versioned and demonstrably integrated for browser-side question generation; the implementer documents the chosen method, training data provenance, licenses and tradeoffs. A prompt-only swap or a hardcoded question carousel is not enough.
3. Quiz items have a single independently checkable correct answer; invalid/ambiguous outputs are rejected or safely replaced, and automated tests exercise failure and diversity cases.
4. Automated, reproducible evaluations compare the adapted approach against a baseline and report quality, output validity, repetition, model size, timing, memory as measurable, plus limitations. Do not invent device benchmarks.
5. Browser/mock/unit tests and existing repository site/build/gallery regression checks pass. Unsupported/memory-constrained conditions fail gracefully; no remote inference, paid service or new server backend is introduced.

## Human-device testing is follow-up, NOT a gate

**The user will personally try the merged demo on a Pixel 7a.** The implementation agent is **not expected to possess that phone**, and **must not make Pixel 7a hands-on verification, parental/child playtesting, subjective manual feedback, or proof of success on that particular device a requirement for PR approval, merge or Issue closure**. Implement reasonable browser/device simulations and available automated measurements, document unverified assumptions, finish the implementable task, and let the user's post-merge feedback guide the **next separate Issue**.

## Non-goals

No real-time multiplayer, cloud AI, speech recognition, camera access, account system, parent dashboard or elaborate learning curriculum. Focus on **a small specialized local AI that makes varied, safe, enjoyable three-choice quizzes for a five-year-old**.", "url": "https://github.com/takahirox/sandbox/issues/64", "created_at": "2026-11-27T00:29:57Z", "state": "OPEN", "repository": "takahirox/sandbox", "labels": ["task"], "priority": null, "status": "In Progress", "is_archived": false}, "context": {}, "resources": {}, "allocation": {}, "instruction": null, "run_id": "b6fb7b637c764d2dbfa25710be9f6489"}
